The starting material is a methyl ketone on a cyclohexane ring, C₆H₁₁–CO–CH₃.
Step 1 — PCl₅ replaces the carbonyl oxygen by two chlorines on the same carbon:
C₆H₁₁–CO–CH₃ + PCl₅ ⇒ C₆H₁₁–CCl₂–CH₃ + POCl₃
P is the gem-dichloride, with both chlorines on one carbon.
Step 2 — sodamide in **excess** is a very strong base and eliminates HCl twice over.
The first elimination gives a vinyl chloride, C₆H₁₁–CCl=CH₂; the second removes the remaining
HCl to leave a carbon–carbon triple bond:
Q = C₆H₁₁–C≡CH
The word 'excess' is the clue: one equivalent would stop at the alkene, two gives the alkyne.
∴ Q is the cyclohexyl alkyne, option (3).

Cryolite is Na₃AlF₆, and it is added to the Hall–Héroult cell for two reasons at once.
Pure alumina melts at about 2323 K, far too hot to electrolyse economically. Dissolving it in
molten cryolite brings the working temperature down to roughly 1223 K — the melting point is
lowered.
Molten alumina on its own is also a poor conductor. Cryolite dissociates into ions and makes
the melt far more conducting, so the cell can be run at a workable voltage.
Fluorspar, CaF₂, is usually added as well to lower the temperature further.
So the answer must mention **both** effects, which is what rules out (2), mentioning only the
melting point, and (1), which says conductivity is *decreased* — the opposite.
∴ it lowers the melting point and increases the conductivity.

Apply VSEPR to each, counting bond pairs and lone pairs on xenon.
XeF₂ — 2 bond pairs, 3 lone pairs, 5 domains ⇒ linear.
XeF₄ — 4 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs, 6 domains ⇒ square planar.
XeOF₄ — 5 bond pairs, 1 lone pair, 6 domains ⇒ square pyramidal.
XeO₃ — xenon has 8 valence electrons; three double bonds to oxygen use six of them, leaving
one lone pair. So 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 4 domains.
Four domains give a tetrahedral arrangement, and with one position occupied by the lone pair
the three oxygens form a **pyramid** below the xenon.
This is the same shape as ammonia, and for the same reason: the lone pair pushes the bonds
down, giving O–Xe–O angles of about 103°.
∴ XeO₃.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|45||0|0:
Both elevation of boiling point and depression of freezing point depend on the same molality,
so find the molality from one and use it in the other.
The freezing point falls from 0 °C to −0.186 °C, so ΔTf = 0.186 K.
ΔTf = Kf · m
0.186 = 1.86 × m
m = 0.186 / 1.86 = 0.1 mol kg⁻¹
Now use that molality with the ebullioscopic constant:
ΔTb = Kb · m
ΔTb = 0.521 × 0.1 = 0.0521 K
The solute is non-volatile and does not dissociate, so i = 1 throughout and no correction is needed.
Notice ΔTb is much the smaller of the two — Kb for water is about a quarter of Kf, which is why
freezing point depression is the more sensitive measurement.
∴ ΔTb = 0.0521 K.

Two substances cannot coexist in solution if they react with each other.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate still has an acidic hydrogen on the HCO₃⁻ ion, and sodium hydroxide
is a strong base, so they neutralise one another at once:
NaHCO₃ + NaOH ⇒ Na₂CO₃ + H₂O
Whichever is in deficit is consumed completely, so the two can never be present together.
The others are all compatible:
(2) NaHCO₃ simply dissolves in water.
(3) NaHCO₃ and Na₂CO₃ together are the standard carbonate–bicarbonate buffer, widely used.
(4) Na₂CO₃ and NaOH are both basic and do not react with each other.
∴ NaHCO₃ and NaOH cannot exist together.

Convert molecules to moles, then moles to mass.
moles = number of molecules / Avogadro's number
= 1.8 × 10²² / 6.022 × 10²³
= 0.0299 ≈ 0.03 mol
Dioxygen is O₂, so its molar mass is 2 × 16 = 32 g mol⁻¹ (not 16 — that is the atom).
mass = moles × molar mass
= 0.03 × 32
= 0.96 g
The usual error is using 16 g mol⁻¹, which halves the answer to 0.48 g, or slipping a factor of
ten and reaching 9.60 g.
∴ 0.960 g.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|49||0|0:
Fill the molecular orbitals and read off bond order and magnetism.
Neutral O₂ has 16 electrons, with two unpaired in the π* orbitals, giving bond order 2.
O₂⁺ — one electron removed, 15 electrons. The electron comes out of a π* antibonding orbital.
Bond order = (10 − 5)/2 = 2.5, and one unpaired electron remains in π* ⇒ paramagnetic.
O₂⁻ — one electron added, 17 electrons, going into π*.
Bond order = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5, and again one unpaired electron in π* ⇒ paramagnetic.
Now test the statements.
(1) True — 2.5 > 1.5.
(2) True — the lower bond order makes O₂⁻ the less stable.
(4) True — both have exactly one unpaired electron.
(3) False — O₂⁺ is **not** diamagnetic. Removing one electron from the two in π* leaves one
behind, still unpaired, so O₂⁺ is paramagnetic just like O₂⁻.
∴ statement (3) is incorrect.
